newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Swiss banks could hold keys to computing security.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Swiss banks could hold keys to computing security.

text.p: Swiss banks are discussing how they can build on their reputation for secrecy by creating a potentially lucrative business guarding codes that unlock encrypted information for customers anywhere in the world.
Bankers say the scheme is in its infancy and that an inter-bank group studying the issue will meet in December to discuss what strategy to pursue.

"Security is not a product, it's a process. The Swiss understand more about it than most because of their fanatical devotion to it for 50 years or more," said Robert Hall, a financial systems specialist at Sun Microsystems Inc.

Swiss financiers have started thinking about forming an independent company owned by banks, which could hold "keys" for decoding encrypted information that customers want to protect from snooping competitors and disloyal employees, he said.

But several legal and technological issues have to be settled before this "key escrow" business can get going. (Escrow is a bank account kept by a third party on behalf of two others in dispute over its ownership).
Hall gave the hypothetical example of a Brazilian bank that would hold two keys internally but seek a trusted third party to keep the third as a safety measure.

"Now whom can you trust?" he asked, holding out Switzerland as a logical candidate because of its vaunted tradition of secrecy, its neutrality, its well-developed financial infrastructure and its relaxed export controls.

"Swiss banks recognise that this is an opportunity. Some of them think there will be a huge export business for security in the future," he said, pointing to the importance of having an external authority to certify important data is authentic.
"It's complicated but the Swiss banks have really thought it through and put it into practice. Their experience is something they will sell," he told Reuters.
SWISS AN OBVIOUS CHOICE
Armand Martin at Credit Suisse in Zurich said Swiss banks were not yet at the stage of marketing themselves as key escrow agents, but he said they would be a logical choice.

"It must be an absolutely neutral, trustworthy place, and in this sense Switzerland is not badly placed because stability prevails in our country and the trustworthiness is there," he said, noting that banks already act as depositories for confidential computer source codes that help form software programmes.

The big question is whether legislators will accept the idea or instead insist on limiting the complexity of encryption programmes to make sure sophisticated criminals cannot outwit law enforcement and intelligence agencies, Martin added.

"The Americans above all are very cautious. The National Security Agency has a big interest in seeing that absolute confidentiality cannot be produced," he said of the super-secret U.S. agency worried about its ability to gather information.

The case for entrusting outsiders with a key to sensitive data is built on the fear of a security breach from within. This poses a far greater risk than common worries about the safety of Internet transactions, Hall said.
"It turns out that people are very concerned about Internet-based electronic commerce. (But) you can totally secure that. It's a done deal. It exists today," he said.

"The firewall stuff is good. It's not watertight. Nothing is watertight. But it is very, very good. The attack will come from the inside. Some employee will sell the keys or there will be internal sabotage. How do you protect against that? That is one of the reasons you might want an external party involved."
Swiss banks are among the leaders in securing sensitive information, he added, putting them ahead of other offshore centres that could compete for the business.

"They have a wealth of experience in understanding how to create security architecture. In the last 20 years they have invested a huge amount of money in understanding IT (information technology) security, and, in the past five years, network security. These other countries don't have the experience."
RUSSIANS WORLD LEADERS IN SECURITY
The Swiss still lag behind the Russians, world leaders in guarding data from intruders.
"Russia has better security architects than anyone in the world. They have a special gene," said Hall, who used to run Sun's Russian operations.
"That is why the U.S. doesn't try to restrict exportation of cryptography to Russia because theirs is better than ours, but nobody is going to trust the Russians. You can trust the Swiss."
Not everyone shares Hall's enthusiasm that the key escrow service has the potential to be a huge business.

"There is only a business opportunity if a government forces organisations or companies to have an external key escrow agent," said Rainer Rueppel, head of R3 Security Engineering AG, a Swiss company studying the issue for the European Union.
"A big organisation like a bank itself would always try to keep this key recovery centre or key escrow centre internal."
The hypothetical Brazilian bank could be just as safe by simply renting a safety deposit box, he said.
"They could achieve the same level of protection by putting that key with a chip card into a safe," he contended, adding: "It sounds a little futuristic."
